title: Split a Word Into Smaller and Smaller Lyndon Words

concept.title: Duval's algorithm grows a periodic block while the letters keep pace with it, and cuts off whole copies of the block when they stop
body: A *Lyndon word* is a non-empty word that is **strictly smaller than all its proper suffixes** (equivalently, than all its rotations): `a`, `ab`, `aab`, `abb` are Lyndon words, `ba` and `abab` are not. Every word can be written in exactly one way as `w1 w2 ... wk` with every `wi` a Lyndon word and `w1 >= w2 >= ... >= wk`. For `bababa` the factorization is `b`, `ab`, `ab`, `a`.

Duval's algorithm finds the factorization in one pass. It keeps a position `i` (the start of the not yet cut part), a scanner `j` and a pointer `k` into the current block: the part `s[i..j)` has the form `u^m u'` where `u` is a Lyndon word and `u'` is a prefix of `u`. Look at the next letter `s[j]` and compare it with `s[k]`, the letter that would continue the periodic pattern. If `s[k] < s[j]`, the block `s[i..j]` becomes a single Lyndon word, so `k = i`. If they are equal, the pattern continues: `k += 1`. If `s[k] > s[j]`, the word cannot be extended; cut off all the **full copies** of `u` (each of length `j - k`) and restart from the first letter after them.

body.code:
i = 0
lengths = []
while i < n:
    j, k = i + 1, i
    while j < n and s[k] <= s[j]:
        k = i if s[k] < s[j] else k + 1
        j += 1
    while i <= k:                  # cut the copies of the Lyndon word of length j - k
        lengths.append(j - k)
        i += j - k
print(len(lengths), *lengths)

body: Each letter is looked at a constant number of times, so the algorithm is O(n) in time and O(1) in extra memory. The same algorithm gives the smallest rotation (the start of the last factor of the doubled word), and it is the base of several string algorithms such as the construction of suffix arrays by sorting.

statement: A Lyndon word is a non-empty word that is strictly smaller than each of its proper suffixes. Every word `s` can be written uniquely as a concatenation of Lyndon words that do not increase: `w1 >= w2 >= ... >= wk`. Print `k` and then the lengths of `w1, ..., wk` on one line.
outputFormat: Print `k` followed by the `k` lengths of the factors, all on one line.
constraints: The word consists of lowercase English letters.

examples.note: The factors are b, ab, ab and a: four factors of the lengths 1, 2, 2, 1, so the output is 4 1 2 2 1.

hints: A factor is as long as possible; the factors do not increase.
Keep i (start), j (scanner) and k (the matching place in the block).
When s[k] > s[j], cut off the copies of the block of length j - k.

explanation: Duval's algorithm scans the word keeping the start of the uncut part, a scanner and a pointer inside the current Lyndon block; when the scanner letter is smaller than the pointer letter, all full copies of the block are cut off.

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

s = input().strip()

n = len(s)
i = 0
lengths = []
while i < n:
    j = i + 1
    k = i
    while j < n and s[k] <= s[j]:
        if s[k] < s[j]:
            k = i
        else:
            k += 1
        j += 1
    while i <= k:
        lengths.append(j - k)
        i += j - k
print(len(lengths), *lengths)
